chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurara, from someone else, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'Is the wiping upon the two socks [done] in dissimulation (taqiyyah)?' He said, 'Dissimulation is not done in three [matters].' I said, 'And what are they?' He said, 'Drinking wine,' or he said, 'Drinking the intoxicant, and the wiping upon the two socks, and Mut'at al-Hajj.'

key_terms.الْمَسْحُ عَلَى الْخُفَّيْنِ: Wiping over the two socks; a method of partial ablution (wudu) where one wipes over leather socks instead of washing the feet.
key_terms.تَقِيَّةٌ: Dissimulation; concealing one's true belief or practice to avoid harm.
key_terms.شُرْبُ الْخَمْرِ: Drinking wine; referring to the consumption of intoxicants.
key_terms.مُتْعَةُ الْحَجِّ: Mut'at al-Hajj; a specific type of marriage contract performed during the pilgrimage season.

ai.seo_question: What are the three matters in which dissimulation (taqiyyah) is not applied according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the ritual wiping upon the socks (*masah al-khufayn*) is a fixed legal ruling rather than a matter of dissimulation (*taqiyyah*), thereby establishing its permanence in Shia jurisprudence. He identifies three specific acts where *taqiyyah* is not applied: drinking wine (or intoxicants), wiping upon the socks, and *Mut'at al-Hajj* (the temporary marriage contract during pilgrimage). This enumeration highlights the distinct status of these practices, particularly affirming the validity of *Masah al-Khufayn* as a core component of ablution that does not require concealment even in times of political pressure.
